newsitem.title: UK: Daiwa's Schmidt warns of Russia power vacuum.
newsitem.headline: Daiwa's Schmidt warns of Russia power vacuum.

text.p: A renewed spate of ill health for President Boris Yeltsin and uncertainty over whether he will face, let alone survive, a heart bypass operation is creating a power struggle in Russia, Daiwa Institute of Research said on Wednesday.

"The president's poor health and forthcoming heart surgery has created a power vacuum. In addition it would seem that the key figures are consolidating their power base and preparing for the top position in a post-Yeltsin era," Daiwa's chief political analyst Susanne Schmidt said in a report.

Most western analysts have assumed that if Yeltsin dies or is incapacitated, Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin will rule for three months and then win a presidential election. But Schmidt warns that his powers at present are limited to the economic arena and there are others who want to exercise their influence.

"Overlapping and/or competing responsibilities are mainly apparent between the power ministries (defence, interior, foreign affairs) on the one hand and the various councils (security, defence, presidential administration) on the other, but also between the power ministries themselves," Schmidt said.
Citing Chechnya as an example, Schmidt says that everyone, from the president to the prime minister and the security chief Alexander Lebed, has some influence.
She also says a temporary transfer of power from Yeltsin to Chernomyrdin would not be as complete as many analysts and commentators have assumed.
"The constitution says nothing about temporary incapacitation. In effect, a new ambiguous muddle has been created which will do nothing to make decisions speedier or more transparent," Schmidt said.
She outlines three alternative scenarios -- successful surgery and a complete recovery, partial recuperation, or death.
Under the first, reforms, including tax, social stabilisation and an increased emphasis on growth and investment are likely to occur.
A partial recovery will leave Chernomyrdin, former prime minister Anatoly Chubais and Lebed in control of considerable chunks of the government.
Schmidt believes there "could be a long period of inertia with necessary political and/or legislative intitiatives being subsumed under an ongoig power struggle".
If surgery leaves Yeltsin dead or permanently incapacitated, a new election must be held within three months.

Most western analysts believe Russia's June presidential elections killed off the communist threat, but Schmidt says Gennady Zyuganov still has solid support, while Chernomyrdin's Our Home is Russia party won just 9.9 percent of the vote in December's parliamentary election.

A defeat for Chernomyrdin could open the way to a contest bewteen Lebed and Zyuganov. "This would leave the direction and pace of future reforms open," Schmidt said. -- David Chance London newsroom 44 171 542 5887
